Benjamin Franklin. An American polymath and statesman whose versatility and diplomatic skill made him indispensable to the American Revolution and the founding of the nation. A printer, inventor, scientist, and philosopher, Franklin embodied Enlightenment values and served as a bridge between the colonial cause and European powers, particularly France. His pragmatism and charm secured crucial foreign support without which American independence would have failed.

Franklin was born in Boston in seventeen six to a large family of modest means. He founded his own printing business in Philadelphia and became wealthy through newspapers, printing, and the Poor Richard's Almanack. He pioneered scientific investigation of electricity through the famous kite experiment around seventeen fifty-two, proving lightning was electrical and inventing the lightning rod. These were practical applications of theoretical inquiry.

Franklin founded the Junto, a civic improvement society, and helped establish Philadelphia's library, the first lending library in America, as well as a hospital and an academy that became the predecessor to the University of Pennsylvania. He represented colonial interests in London as a diplomatic agent, becoming a voice for American grievances against British policy before and during the Revolutionary War.

Franklin was the key negotiator of the Treaty of Paris in seventeen eighty-three, securing American independence and advantageous territorial terms for the new nation. His reputation and French connections were essential to victory. He served as a delegate to the Constitutional Convention in seventeen eighty-seven and supported ratification of the Constitution, despite having reservations. His support helped forge consensus during the founding of the republic.
